title: What is the difference between batch and stream processing engines (e.g. Spark batch vs Spark Structured Streaming / Flink), and when do you use micro-batch vs true record-at-a-time streaming?
shortTitle: Batch vs stream processing engines, and micro-batch vs record-at-a-time

s1_definition.profdef: A batch engine like Spark batch processes a bounded dataset in scheduled runs, optimizing for throughput and cost. A stream engine processes an unbounded dataset continuously; Spark Structured Streaming does this as micro-batches (small groups of records processed at short intervals), while Flink processes true record-at-a-time (each event individually). Micro-batch gives high throughput with a small latency floor and simpler semantics, whereas record-at-a-time gives the lowest latency and finer-grained state at the cost of more complexity.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India can total transactions three ways. A batch engine is the night shift totalling the whole day's pile at once. Spark Structured Streaming's micro-batch is like a clerk who scoops up whatever slips landed in the last half-second and processes that little scoop, then the next scoop — continuous, but in tiny stacks. Flink's record-at-a-time is a clerk who processes each slip the exact instant it touches the counter, never waiting to form a stack. Night-shift batch is cheapest for big reports; scoops are a great balance for most streaming; and per-slip is the choice when every millisecond counts, like blocking a fraudulent swipe instantly.
s1_definition.oneliner: Batch processes finished chunks on a schedule, micro-batch processes tiny continuous stacks with a small latency floor, and record-at-a-time processes each event instantly for the lowest latency.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A batch engine like Spark batch processes a bounded dataset in scheduled runs, optimizing for throughput and cost. A stream engine processes an unbounded dataset continuously; Spark Structured Streaming does this as micro-batches (small groups of records processed at short intervals), while Flink processes true record-at-a-time (each event individually). Micro-batch gives high throughput with a small latency floor and simpler semantics, whereas record-at-a-time gives the lowest latency and finer-grained state at the cost of more complexity.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India can total transactions three ways. A batch engine is the night shift totalling the whole day's pile at once. Spark Structured Streaming's micro-batch is like a clerk who scoops up whatever slips landed in the last half-second and processes that little scoop, then the next scoop — continuous, but in tiny stacks. Flink's record-at-a-time is a clerk who processes each slip the exact instant it touches the counter, never waiting to form a stack. Night-shift batch is cheapest for big reports; scoops are a great balance for most streaming; and per-slip is the choice when every millisecond counts, like blocking a fraudulent swipe instantly.

**One line to remember:** Batch processes finished chunks on a schedule, micro-batch processes tiny continuous stacks with a small latency floor, and record-at-a-time processes each event instantly for the lowest latency.

sections.s2_technical:
A batch engine works on a bounded dataset with a known end. Spark batch reads an entire chunk, builds an optimized plan, runs it, writes the result, and stops until the next scheduled run. Because it sees all the data, it does large joins and full aggregations efficiently and is trivial to re-run, which suits end-of-day reports and historical backfills. The downside is latency: results are only as fresh as the schedule.

Stream engines process an unbounded dataset continuously, but they differ in how. Spark Structured Streaming uses a micro-batch model: it treats the stream as a series of small bounded batches, triggering every short interval, so under the hood it reuses Spark's batch engine and optimizer on tiny slices. This gives very high throughput and the same familiar DataFrame API as batch, which is a big operational advantage, but it carries a latency floor equal to roughly the trigger interval, often hundreds of milliseconds to a few seconds. Spark later added a lower-latency continuous mode, but micro-batch is the common one. A Structured Streaming query reads almost identically to batch: `spark.readStream.format("kafka")...groupBy(window($"ts","1 minute"), $"accountId").sum("amount").writeStream...start()`.

Flink uses a true record-at-a-time model: each event flows through operators individually, so latency can be in the low milliseconds. This finer granularity gives precise event-time handling, rich keyed state updated per event, and exactly-once via checkpoint barriers, which makes Flink the stronger choice for complex stateful streaming and the lowest-latency needs. The trade-off is that record-at-a-time systems are typically more complex to operate and reason about than reusing a batch engine.

Choosing between them is about latency, throughput, state complexity, and operational simplicity. You use batch when freshness is not critical and cost and simplicity win, like nightly reporting and backfills. You use micro-batch when near-real-time, say a couple of seconds, is good enough and you value one unified API and operational familiarity, which covers a large fraction of streaming use cases. You use true record-at-a-time when you need the lowest latency, sophisticated per-event stateful logic, or the strongest event-time semantics, like real-time fraud blocking. A senior nuance is that the line has blurred: Spark narrowed its latency with continuous processing and Flink supports batch over bounded streams, so the decision often comes down to your latency budget, how complex your state is, and which engine your team already operates well. In a bank I typically run batch for reporting, micro-batch for most near-real-time dashboards and enrichment, and reserve Flink for the latency-critical, heavily stateful fraud and risk jobs.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The bank needs a nightly complete total. This is exactly batch — process the whole bounded day at once.

Problem 2 — A near-real-time dashboard needs updates every short interval and the team wants a simple unified API. This is exactly micro-batch — process small continuous stacks of events.

Problem 3 — Fraud blocking needs the lowest possible latency per event. This is exactly record-at-a-time — handle each event instantly.

The mini-project simulates all three engines on the same events. `BatchEngine` totals a whole bounded list in one run. `MicroBatchEngine` buffers events and processes them in small fixed-size stacks with a per-stack latency note. `RecordAtATimeEngine` processes each event immediately. The demo runs the same transactions through all three and contrasts the latency and grouping behaviour.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is five transactions for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001), one of Priya's being 150000 which crosses the fraud threshold.

Step 1 — Batch engine. The batch engine treats the five transactions as a complete bounded set and makes one pass, producing final totals: Rajesh 1200 + 800 + 300 = 2300, Priya 150000 + 5000 = 155000. This is the night-shift style, complete but only at run time.

Step 2 — Micro-batch, first stack. The micro-batch engine buffers until it has two events, then processes that small stack. After the first stack of the first two transactions, running totals already reflect Rajesh 1200 and Priya 150000, and the engine notes a latency floor around the trigger interval.

Step 3 — Micro-batch, remaining stacks. The next two transactions form the second stack, updating running totals, and the final single transaction forms a small last stack. The results emerge continuously in tiny increments rather than all at once.

Step 4 — Record-at-a-time, instant decisions. The record engine processes each transaction the instant it arrives. Priya's 150000 immediately triggers a low-latency fraud alert, while the others log as ok, each acted upon individually with no waiting to form a stack.

Step 5 — Contrast. All three produced correct account behaviour, but batch gave one complete answer at run time, micro-batch gave continuous near-real-time updates with a small latency floor, and record-at-a-time gave the instant per-event reaction needed for fraud blocking.

```

INFO: CUR3001 = 155000
INFO: === MICRO-BATCH ENGINE (small continuous stacks) ===

INFO: MICRO-BATCH #2 processed 2 rows (latency floor ~ trigger interval), running={SAV2001=2000, CUR3001=155000}
INFO: MICRO-BATCH #3 processed 1 rows (latency floor ~ trigger interval), running={SAV2001=2300, CUR3001=155000}
INFO: === RECORD-AT-A-TIME ENGINE (instant per event) ===
INFO: RECORD-AT-A-TIME ok: SAV2001 1200
SEVERE: RECORD-AT-A-TIME low-latency ALERT: CUR3001 150000 (acted instantly)
INFO: RECORD-AT-A-TIME ok: SAV2001 800
INFO: RECORD-AT-A-TIME ok: CUR3001 5000
INFO: RECORD-AT-A-TIME ok: SAV2001 300
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Same 5 transactions
    │
    ├─ BATCH                 ├─ MICRO-BATCH (Spark SS)      ├─ RECORD-AT-A-TIME (Flink)
    │  wait for whole set    │  stack of 2 → process        │  event1 → act now
    │  one pass              │  stack of 2 → process        │  event2 → ALERT now
    │  final totals          │  stack of 1 → process        │  event3 → act now
    ▼                        ▼                              ▼
  complete @ run time       continuous, ~trigger latency    instant, lowest latency
  SAV=2300 CUR=155000       running totals update per stack  per-event fraud decision
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A batch engine like Spark batch processes a bounded dataset in scheduled runs, reading the whole chunk, building an optimized plan, running it, and stopping until the next schedule, which makes it efficient for large joins and aggregations, trivial to re-run, and ideal for end-of-day reports and backfills, with the only cost being that results are only as fresh as the schedule. Stream engines process an unbounded dataset continuously, but they differ in how. Spark Structured Streaming uses a micro-batch model, treating the stream as a series of tiny bounded batches triggered every short interval, which reuses Spark's batch engine and gives the same familiar DataFrame API and very high throughput, but carries a latency floor roughly equal to the trigger interval. Flink uses true record-at-a-time processing, flowing each event through operators individually so latency can be in the low milliseconds, with precise event-time handling, rich per-event keyed state, and exactly-once via checkpoint barriers, at the cost of being more complex to operate.

Choosing between them comes down to latency, throughput, state complexity, and operational simplicity. I use batch when freshness is not critical and cost and simplicity win. I use micro-batch when near-real-time of a second or two is good enough and I value one unified API and operational familiarity, which covers a large share of streaming use cases. I use true record-at-a-time when I need the lowest latency, sophisticated per-event stateful logic, or the strongest event-time semantics. A senior point I add is that the line has blurred, since Spark added a lower-latency continuous mode and Flink supports batch over bounded streams, so the real decision is my latency budget, how complex my state is, and which engine my team already runs well.

In my project at the National Bank of India I split the work along exactly these lines. Nightly reports and historical backfills ran on Spark batch for completeness and low cost. Near-real-time dashboards and enrichment ran on Spark Structured Streaming's micro-batch because a couple of seconds was fine and the unified API kept the team productive. And the latency-critical, heavily stateful fraud and risk jobs ran on Flink, where processing each swipe the instant it arrived let us block a fraudulent transaction immediately rather than a few seconds later. Matching the engine to the workload is what kept the platform both cost-effective and fast where it mattered.
